title: Should you regress the levels? The ADF test, read properly

explain.prompt: Your colleague wants to regress log WTI on log Brent in levels. Using the test-code output, explain in 6–8 sentences: H0 and H1 of ADF; what the results on log Brent, log WTI, their returns and the log spread imply (orders of integration); why p = 0.15 on log Brent does NOT prove a unit root; why the trend-stationary example needs 'ct'; what the short-sample and level-shift examples teach; and what the lag choice changes. Conclude: can the levels be regressed with ordinary OLS inference?
rubric: ADF regression Δy_t = [c] + [bt] + γ y_{t−1} + lagged Δy + e; H0: γ = 0 (unit root), H1: γ < 0 (stationary around 0 / a level / a trend). The statistic follows the Dickey-Fuller distribution (5 % critical value ≈ −2.87 with a constant), not Student's t.

Log Brent and log WTI: no rejection (p ≈ 0.15 and 0.19); their daily returns: strong rejection → each price behaves as I(1) (a random walk: shocks are permanent). The log spread rejects strongly (p ≈ 0) → I(0): a stationary combination, i.e. a candidate cointegration with β ≈ 1.

p > 0.05 is absence of evidence against H0, not evidence for it: ADF has low power — the 40-observation stationary series is not rejected (p ≈ 0.52), and a stationary series with a level shift is not rejected either (p ≈ 0.47): breaks fool the test.

Deterministic terms must match the series: the trend-stationary simulation looks like a unit root with 'c' (p ≈ 0.86) and is clearly stationary with 'ct' (p ≈ 0) — choose from the chart and the economics, not by trying all options; 'n' for series centred on zero (returns, residuals).
Lags whiten the residuals: too few bias the test, too many cost power; AIC chooses here, and the conclusion should not hinge on one particular lag.

Conclusion: both levels are I(1) → ordinary OLS inference in levels is invalid (spurious-regression risk, step 4.6); a level relationship is only meaningful if the residual is stationary — test cointegration (4.7).
